titre: The HeLa Line, Taken Without a Word
accroche: In 1951, a fragment of tumor taken without asking its patient becomes the first line of human cells that never stopped dividing.
contenu_vulgarise:
In 1951, Henrietta Lacks, 30, a mother of five, is diagnosed at Johns Hopkins Hospital in Baltimore with a cervical cancer of unusual aggressiveness. Fragments of her tumor are taken for research and handed to the biologist George Gey, without her being informed, without anyone asking her. At the time, this was common practice.

What Gey observes next is unprecedented. For a long time, researchers had been trying without success to keep human cells alive outside the body: those taken before survived only a few days. Some of Henrietta's cells, though, behave differently. Gey isolates one, multiplies it, and the line is born. It takes the name HeLa, formed from the first two letters of the patient's first and last names, which was meant to protect her identity. Cancer kills Henrietta Lacks on October 4, 1951, at 31, after spreading throughout her body. Her cell line, for its part, has never stopped.

## A cell factory in Alabama

In October 1952, the research director of the American foundation against infantile paralysis (the NFIP) asks Russell W. Brown, who heads the Carver Research Foundation at the Tuskegee Institute in Alabama, to turn his premises into the world's first HeLa cell factory. The aim is to test Jonas Salk's vaccine on a large scale. In a glass dish, you put HeLa cells, the blood of a vaccinated person and a small dose of poliovirus: if the needed antibodies are missing, the cells become deformed, and you can see it under the microscope. But the trial would require 10,000 tubes of cells every week. Brown is assisted by James H. M. Henderson, and Norma Gaillard, who supervises cell culture, develops a procedure that her technicians follow to the letter. The team ends up exceeding those 10,000 tubes, shipped by air to about twenty laboratories across the country. The Salk vaccine trial starts on April 26, 1954 and involves about 1.6 million children, in Canada, Finland and the United States. The results are announced on April 12, 1955.

## A file never closed

Henrietta Lacks's cells have since been used for the polio vaccine, for the study of cancer, viruses and the effects of radiation, and for in vitro fertilization. Her family, for its part, remained ignorant of the cell line for more than twenty-five years, and never received any financial benefit from the industry it helped found.

In 2013, researchers at the European Molecular Biology Laboratory in Germany publish the complete HeLa genome sequence online. Criticism over privacy and the family's consent is immediate, and the sequence is withdrawn almost at once: the question posed in 1951 had never really been closed. The director of the National Institutes of Health meets with the family, and an agreement is reached: NIH-funded researchers who sequence HeLa lines must deposit their data in a controlled-access database, and a committee that includes direct descendants of Henrietta Lacks reviews access requests. More than sixty years after a sample taken without a word, it is her descendants who decide who can open the file.

repere.texte: About 1.6 million children, in Canada, Finland and the United States, took part in the Salk polio vaccine trial, the results of which the WHO dates to the announcement of April 12, 1955.
repere.source: World Health Organization, “History of polio vaccination”

carte.punch: Her cells were used to test the Salk vaccine. Nobody had asked her anything.
carte.idee: In 1951, a fragment of Henrietta Lacks's tumor is taken without informing her. The human cells cultured until then survived only a few days; one of hers did not. It is used to test the polio vaccine. Her family is kept in the dark for more than twenty-five years, with no financial benefit.

quiz.question: Why did the cells taken from Henrietta Lacks in 1951 mark a turning point for biological research?
choix: They made it possible to sequence the very first complete human genome from a tumor
They divided indefinitely in culture, whereas earlier human cells died within a few days
They were the very first human cells observed under an electron microscope
They came from the very first documented organ donation in the United States
quiz.explication: Before 1951, human cells taken for culture survived only a few days outside the body. A cell isolated from Henrietta Lacks's tumor kept dividing without stopping, which made it the first “immortal” human cell line and a research tool reproducible indefinitely, hence its massive use, from the polio vaccine to research today. The other answers are wrong: the first complete human genome was not sequenced from these cells, they were not the first observed under an electron microscope, and they do not come from an organ donation.

quiz_supplementaire.question: What role did the Tuskegee Institute play in the story of HeLa cells?
choix: It developed the polio vaccine tested starting in 1954
It housed the world's first HeLa cell factory
It kept Henrietta Lacks's medical file until 2013
It trained the Johns Hopkins researchers who took the sample
quiz_supplementaire.explication: Russell W. Brown, with James H. M. Henderson and Norma Gaillard, turned the Carver Research Foundation's laboratory there into a cell factory, which ended up exceeding 10,000 culture tubes a week, shipped by air to about twenty laboratories across the country. The vaccine itself was developed by Jonas Salk.

quiz_supplementaire.question: What did the National Institutes of Health obtain after the publication of the HeLa genome in 2013?
choix: The withdrawal of all HeLa lines from American laboratories
Payment to the Lacks family of a share of the industry's revenue
An agreement placing the data under controlled access, with a committee including family members
A permanent ban on sequencing the line's genome again
quiz_supplementaire.explication: NIH-funded researchers who sequence HeLa lines must deposit their data in a controlled-access database, and a committee that includes direct descendants of Henrietta Lacks reviews the requests. The family, however, obtained no financial benefit from this industry.

quiz_supplementaire.question: Where does the name “HeLa” come from?
choix: From the first two letters of Henrietta Lacks's first and last names
From the name of the biologist George Gey, who first cultured these cells
From the Johns Hopkins hospital department where the tumor was taken
From the serial number assigned to the sample in the laboratory register
quiz_supplementaire.explication: The name takes the first two letters of the patient's first and last names, Henrietta Lacks, which was meant to protect her identity: her family was unaware of the line's existence for more than twenty-five years. It therefore comes neither from the biologist George Gey, nor from a hospital department, nor from a register number.
